newsitem.title: CANADA: Arakis CEO sees little spending in '97-98.
newsitem.headline: Arakis CEO sees little spending in '97-98.

text.p: Arakis Energy Corp, which signed official agreements for its Sudan oil project last weekend, expects to spend little of its own cash reserves on the development over the next two years, Arakis chief executive John McLeod said on Tuesday.
"Our cash commitments for 1997 and 1998 under this agreement are very, very near to zero," McLeod told a conference call.
He said the company would pay signing and training bonuses to the government of Sudan valued at about US$1 million as part of the agreement.
"Other than that, we have credit for the money we have spent plus the value that was added...which should effectively carry us through 1998 with very little cash draw," he said.

Arakis and its partners on Saturday signed the final agreements for the project, which includes exploration and development drilling in the southern Sudan blocks and a 1,500 km pipeline to the Red Sea from the oil fields.

Partners in the development include Arakis with 25 percent, China National Petroleum Corp with 40 percent, Malaysia state oil company Petronas with 30 percent and the Khartoum government with five percent.

Under the agreement, Arakis was to be credited for US$100 million for the upstream expenditures it has made on the lands over the past three years, as well as further amounts for improvements of the blocks and spending on the pipeline plans, McLeod said.
The total credited amount would likely be "in the magnitude" of US$200 million, he said.
He said the pipeline could be in operation midway through 1999 and he expected that Arakis's cash flow per share would be US$2 based on an initial production rate of 150,000 barrels of oil per day.
McLeod said that Arakis had bought back about 0.5 percent of its outstanding shares under its current issuer bid, which was launched in December.

Addressing confusion over the past few days regarding varying reserve estimates for the project put forward by the different partners, McLeod said he continued to be comfortable with proven plus probable and potential reserves of over 600 million barrels and said he believed the figure was conservative.
The partners planned a drilling program of 30 development wells and 21 exploration wells between now and startup of the pipeline, he said.
One rig was currently working on the lands and another was in transit to the oil fields from the Port of Sudan. Also, a total of four seismic crews were expected to be gathering data soon, McLeod.
